subtype: Approach: watching others and copying their arm strokes [Action]
passage: At the club pool in Pune, Manav sat on the edge with wet feet and watched Zeenat, the older girl in lane three, cut through the water. Her right arm swung up, her hand slid in, and she pulled. Manav stood on the tiles and copied the movement, arm over arm, in the air. Then he tried it in the water while Bhavna Ma'am walked along the side. "Good reach. Your elbow is dropping, Manav. Lift it first, like Zeenat does." He lifted it. The stroke felt strange, but the splash was smaller, and he managed a full length without stopping.

qa.q: Whose arm movement did Manav watch before trying the stroke?
qa.a: He watched Zeenat, the older girl in lane three.

qa.q: What was Manav feeling as he tried the stroke in the water with the coach beside him?
qa.a: Curious and a little unsure, because the stroke felt strange, yet he kept going and was pleased when the splash got smaller. 😊

qa.q: What other approach could help Manav see his own elbow, and why?
qa.a: A friend could film a short clip from the poolside, so Manav can watch his elbow and fix it between lessons.

qa.q: How does Bhavna Ma'am see Manav's copying?
qa.a: She sees a good start, since he already has the rough shape of the stroke, and she adds the one missing correction about his elbow.

grounding: A boy studies an older swimmer, copies the arm movement on land and in the water, and the coach corrects his elbow.

subtype: Approach: practising only with a float and never without [Pitfall]
passage:
"Uma, leave the board on the edge today," said Coach Faisal.
"One more length with it first."
"You said that last week. And the week before."
Uma held the kickboard against her chest. "But it keeps me up."
"I know. Here, where you can stand, you could try two kicks without it, and I'll be an arm's reach away."
"What if I sink?"
"Then your feet touch the floor."
She looked at the board, then at the far wall, and shook her head. "Tomorrow."
"That's weeks of tomorrows, Uma. Your kick is lovely. But I have never seen you swim on your own."

qa.q: What did Uma hold against her chest?
qa.a: Uma held the kickboard against her chest.

qa.q: What is Uma afraid of when the coach asks her to try without the board?
qa.a: She fears sinking, as her question "What if I sink?" and her shaken head show.

qa.q: What could Uma try instead, and why might it work?
qa.a: She could let go for two kicks in the shallow water with the coach an arm's reach away, then lengthen it, because she can stand there and the fear has a safety net.

qa.q: How does Coach Faisal see Uma's habit with the board?
qa.a: Coach Faisal sees a lovely kick but no real swimming after weeks, so the board may have become something Uma cannot do without.

grounding: A girl always swims with a kickboard, so after weeks of practice she still cannot swim without it.

subtype: Approach: swimming only when a trained adult is watching [Thinking]
passage: The May afternoon was so hot that the courtyard tiles burned. Jomon's cousins were already running toward the river behind the coconut grove, shouting for him to come. He stopped at the gate. The water looked calm, but he remembered Achan saying that rivers hide currents. "Water doesn't care how well I run," he thought. "If a trained grown-up is watching, I go in. If not, I don't. That's my plan, not my limit." So he called out, "I'll swim on Sunday at the town pool, where Sudha Chechi is the lifeguard!" His cousins groaned, but Jomon was already hunting for his towel, feeling oddly proud.

qa.q: Where did Jomon plan to swim on Sunday?
qa.a: He planned to swim at the town pool, where Sudha Chechi is the lifeguard.

qa.q: How did Jomon feel about staying away from the river?
qa.a: Oddly proud and steady rather than left out, because he sees his rule as a plan and not a limit.

qa.q: What could Jomon suggest to his cousins so they can cool off safely, and why?
qa.a: He could suggest they all go to the pool with the lifeguard, so everyone gets out of the heat with a trained person watching.

qa.q: How might Jomon's cousins see his choice?
qa.a: They groaned, so they may feel he is missing the fun, though Jomon offered another plan and they might later see it as careful.

grounding: A child decides never to enter water without a trained adult watching, and treats this as part of his plan.

subtype: Approach: setting small distances as goals [Revision]
passage:
Monday. Nidhi watched the others race lengths and felt slow. "One width," she told herself. She swam it, touched the wall and grinned, and wrote a 1 in her swim book.
The next Monday she managed two widths, gasping but done. A 2 went in the book.
By the third Monday it was four. Her brother Samir clicked the stopwatch at the wall and said, "Whoa." Nidhi did not care that the others were still faster. She turned back a page and looked at the row of numbers, climbing.

qa.q: How many widths did Nidhi swim on the third Monday?
qa.a: She swam four widths on the third Monday.

qa.q: What was Nidhi feeling on the first Monday as she watched the others?
qa.a: Slow and a little discouraged, which is why she gave herself just one width to do.

qa.q: What other approach could keep Nidhi motivated if progress stalls, and why?
qa.a: She could swim with a friend at her speed and cheer each other's widths, since a shared count helps when her own numbers stop rising.

qa.q: How does Samir see Nidhi's progress?
qa.a: Samir is impressed, as his "Whoa" shows, because he has watched the widths grow week by week.

grounding: A girl who feels slow sets small distance goals, one width then two, and counts her progress each week.

subtype: Approach: writing a list from the teacher's notice [Action]
passage:
Monday. The circular about the museum trip came home in Tarun's bag. He read it twice at the study table, pen in hand.
Tuesday. He copied each item onto a slip: lunch box, water bottle, cap, ID card, fifty rupees. He did not add his football, because the notice never asked for it.
Friday. The bus left at seven. At the gate, Ira Ma'am checked each child and paused at Tarun's bag. "Everything the notice asks for. Good." Tarun grinned and climbed aboard.

qa.q: What items did Tarun write on his slip?
qa.a: He wrote lunch box, water bottle, cap, ID card and fifty rupees.

qa.q: What was Tarun thinking when he left his football off the list?
qa.a: Tarun felt sure and confident, because the notice showed what was needed, so there was no reason to guess.

qa.q: What could Tarun do if part of the circular seemed unclear, and why?
qa.a: He could ask the teacher or a parent to read it with him, since the notice is the source and a second reader can confirm it.

qa.q: How does Ira Ma'am see Tarun's bag at the gate?
qa.a: She sees a child who followed what the notice asked, and she says "Good", so she can move on quickly.

grounding: A boy reads the school notice and builds his packing list from what it states, without guessing.

subtype: Approach: imagining the day from morning to evening [Thinking]
passage: Tuesday night. Trip is on Friday and I keep walking through it in my head like a film. Bus at seven, so breakfast early. Then the walk across the fort courtyard, and that sun is fierce by eleven. Hat! Lunch on the steps, so a napkin and a bag for the wrappers. Then the ride back when everyone is sticky and sneezy. Tissues! I put a hat, a pack of tissues and a bag for the wrappers on my list. Mummy says I sound like a tour guide. 🙂 Now to find my good hat. - Amandeep

qa.q: What three things did Amandeep add after picturing the day?
qa.a: Amandeep added a hat, a pack of tissues and a bag for the wrappers.

qa.q: What might Amandeep be feeling while going through the trip in mind?
qa.a: Excited and careful at once, looking forward to the day and wanting to be ready, and cheerful about the tour guide teasing.

qa.q: What other approach could Amandeep use to check the list, and why?
qa.a: Amandeep could ask a friend who went on a similar trip what they wished they had brought, because that may add things imagining missed.

qa.q: How does Mummy seem to see Amandeep's planning?
qa.a: Mummy finds it a bit funny and impressive, since Mummy says Amandeep sounds like a tour guide.

grounding: A child walks through the trip from morning to evening in the mind and adds items for sun, sniffles and litter.

subtype: Approach: packing at the last minute in a hurry [Pitfall]
passage: Jeevan woke at 6:20 and remembered the trip. At 6:30 he was pulling things out of drawers and stuffing them into his bag: cap, snack, a comic. "Jeevan, the bus!" his mother called. At five to seven he reached the gate, panting, just as the bus turned the corner. On the steps he patted his pockets. No permission slip. No water bottle. Gurpreet Ma'am frowned at her list. Then his mother came running down the lane with both in her hand, out of breath. "Next time, the night before," she said. Jeevan's face burned as he took them.

qa.q: What did Jeevan forget when he left for the bus?
qa.a: He forgot his permission slip and his water bottle.

qa.q: How did Jeevan feel when his mother ran up with the forgotten things?
qa.a: Embarrassed, since his face burned, and probably relieved that he could still go.

qa.q: What could Jeevan do to avoid this rush, and why?
qa.a: He could pack the evening before and check a list in the morning, so there is time to notice anything missing.

qa.q: What might Jeevan's mother be feeling as she runs down the lane?
qa.a: She is likely hurried and worried, out of breath, and perhaps a little annoyed, but she still helps him.

grounding: A child starts packing at 6:30 for a 7 o'clock bus, forgets two key items and his mother has to bring them to the gate.

subtype: Approach: keeping the bag light and taking only what is needed [Thinking]
passage: On the last afternoon before the zoo trip, Ganga Ma'am read out the list. Naveen looked at his big blue backpack under the desk and remembered last time: books, a toy car and two water bottles had dragged at his shoulders until his neck ached by lunch. "This time, only what I will use," he thought. At home that evening he took out the toy car, the storybook and the extra tiffin and put them back on the shelf. He chose the small red bag, put in water, lunch and a cap, and lifted it with one finger. "Easy," he said.

qa.q: What did Naveen take out of his bag?
qa.a: He took out the toy car, the storybook and the extra tiffin.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling as he looked at his big backpack?
qa.a: He was wary of another aching neck like last time, so he felt determined to carry only what he would use.

qa.q: What else could Naveen do to keep his bag light and still be ready, and why?
qa.a: He could ask what the zoo provides, so he does not carry things he can get there.

qa.q: How might Ganga Ma'am see a child with a small bag on a long walking day?
qa.a: She likely sees a child who can keep up all day without tiring, whose bag holds only what he needs.

grounding: A boy remembers how a heavy bag tired him before and decides to carry only what is needed in a small bag.

subtype: Approach: packing the day before and checking twice [Action]
passage: On Thursday evening Sunaina laid everything on her bed in rows and ticked her list: lunch box, water, tissues, notebook. The sun cap was still drying on the balcony rail, so she wrote "morning" beside it and zipped the bag. On Friday, before breakfast, she went down the list again with a pencil. "Sun cap..." It hung there, damp at the edge. "Karthik, towel!" Her brother rubbed it dry while she folded it into the bag. At the bus stop she felt no fluttering in her stomach, only the ordinary morning wind.

qa.q: Where was the sun cap on Thursday evening?
qa.a: It was still drying on the balcony rail.

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling at the bus stop, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt calm, since she felt no fluttering in her stomach after both checks. 🙂

qa.q: What other approach could help Sunaina if she still worried, and why?
qa.a: She could ask a parent to look over her list too, since a second person might notice something she overlooked.

qa.q: How does Karthik help in this scene, and how might he feel about it?
qa.a: Karthik rubs the cap dry with a towel, and probably feels glad to be useful and quick, as he acts as soon as she calls.

grounding: A girl packs the day before and checks the list again in the morning, which catches the sun cap she needed.

subtype: Approach: taking everything he might possibly need [Pitfall]
passage:
Sunday. Arnab lay awake imagining rain, cold, hunger, darkness. In the morning he crammed two jackets, three snacks and his father's big torch into his bag.
Monday. At the school gate the bag dragged him sideways. Leela Ma'am hoisted it and raised an eyebrow. "What is in here, Arnab?" She had him leave half of it in the staff room. He watched a jacket and the torch vanish into a cupboard, feeling silly.
Tuesday. In class Leela Ma'am asked how the trip went. "My shoulders hurt at the start," Arnab said. "I never needed the torch."

qa.q: What did Arnab put in his bag on Sunday?
qa.a: He put in two jackets, three snacks and his father's big torch.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling as the jacket and torch vanished into the cupboard?
qa.a: He felt silly, and probably a little embarrassed, since his worry had loaded him with things that were taken away.

qa.q: What could Arnab try next time instead of packing for everything, and why?
qa.a: He could list the likely needs and ask the teacher what is really needed, so his worry gets a limit and his bag stays light.

qa.q: How does Leela Ma'am see Arnab's packing?
qa.a: She sees a worried child carrying more than he can manage, so she lightens the load kindly and asks about the day afterwards.

grounding: A boy packs for every possible problem, ends up with a heavy bag and has to leave half of it at school.
